segments.title: Why few ships were truly treaty battleships
segments.summary: The introduction warns that "treaty battleship" can be a misleading label because many ships were built as the restrictions were already weakening.
segments.body: Very few capital ships were completed as pure products of stable treaty limits. Many appeared near the end of the era, when navies were already ignoring provisions or preparing to exceed them. The King George V class and contemporary American construction illustrate how designs could contain plans for later displacement or capability growth. The video therefore examines capital ships built during the treaty era, including vessels that did not remain fully compliant throughout their design and service.

evidence.note: The introduction says few capital ships were true treaty products and points to British and American preparations for adding capability as limits weakened.

segments.title: Why a naval treaty needs shared incentives
segments.summary: The treaty discussion frames capital ships as products of a system that works only when every signatory sees enough benefit to uphold it.
segments.body: Treaty success depends on whether every signatory sees enough benefit to keep the agreement. A settlement that visibly humiliates one party gives that party little reason to obey, while strategic aims and domestic perceptions can make the same concession look different to different navies. Even negotiators who obtain their stated demands can lose if those demands fail to deliver the security they expected. The Washington Conference's diplomatic setting also shows how much preparation and private bargaining sits behind the published terms.

evidence.note: The transcript explains equitable treaties, strategic goals, and the Washington Conference context.

segments.title: American eavesdropping at the Washington Conference
segments.summary: American efforts to overhear the delegates reveal both the value and the limits of intelligence during treaty negotiations.
segments.body: The video describes the United States bugging delegates' rooms before the Washington Conference so it could learn other powers' negotiating positions. British Empire representatives, however, met collectively on neutral ground outside the rooms prepared for them, leaving an important part of their discussions beyond the installed microphones. Moving or adding devices after delegates arrived risked exposing the operation and collapsing a conference from which the United States wanted concrete results. The episode shows intelligence collection interacting with diplomatic organization, operational caution, and political risk.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the room bugging, the British Empire group's neutral meeting place, and the risk of discovery.

segments.title: Treaty fears and the naval-race explanation
segments.summary: The Colorado and Nagato building programmes anchor a challenge to the idea that the Washington Treaty simply halted an active postwar naval race or that naval competition alone caused the First World War.
segments.body: The immediate shipbuilding picture includes Maryland already in service, Colorado not yet commissioned, and further American and Japanese hulls under construction. That concrete programme differed from the paper possibility of a future race, and the video rejects the claim that a full building race was already under way in 1921-22. The analysis also separates the Anglo-German quantitative contest from wider political tensions and the qualitative competition among Britain, the United States, Japan, and Italy. The prewar naval race is presented as a symptom of a larger Anglo-German struggle for status and an insufficient cause of the First World War by itself. This makes disarmament policy a response to strategic fear and political history as well as ship totals.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Colorado and Nagato construction baseline, then contrasts an assumed race with the wider causes and forms of naval competition.

segments.title: Hood and Britain’s treaty tonnage advantage
segments.summary: Hood’s exceptional displacement complicates the treaty baseline and helps explain why nominal Anglo-American parity did not translate into identical capital-ship totals.
segments.body: Hood is presented as a battlecruiser whose 41,200-ton standard displacement sits far above the later 35,000-ton treaty limit. Its combination of size and mobility mattered especially in a global war of maneuver, a different problem from replaying a concentrated Jutland-style battle. Comparing British and American allowances shows that Britain retained enough additional capital-ship tonnage to be roughly a Nelson-class ship ahead. The figures illustrate how inherited fleets and permitted replacements shaped practical power behind formal parity.

evidence.note: Hood's displacement and British versus American treaty totals are discussed.

segments.title: A treaty as budget control and security policy
segments.summary: This section compares the peace aims, financial pressures, and security calculations facing Britain, France, Japan, and the United States.
segments.body: The transcript treats Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points and League of Nations as a genuine peace-seeking strand in the effort to restrain armaments. Some governments also wanted relief from naval expenditure. France faced reconstruction and extensive postwar commitments, while Japan worried about the scale of American plans and the infrastructure bill required to match them. Britain expected to build to any agreed ceiling while doubting that the United States would appropriate the money or that other powers could afford to follow. The same treaty limit therefore carried very different meanings for each signatory.

evidence.note: The transcript compares peace aims, national spending, security, and industrial considerations.

segments.title: Britain's postwar economy and battleship affordability
segments.summary: The case for British treaty restraint is separated from the claim that Britain was simply too impoverished to build its planned capital ships.
segments.body: The planned G3 programme is presented as affordable within the scale of the British government's interwar budget. Warship orders would also have supported employment, yards, and industrial activity alongside their direct cost. The wider comparison emphasizes that Britain supplied arms during the First World War and did not suffer the physical devastation imposed on continental Europe, even though it endured debt, casualties, and economic damage. Treaty restraint was therefore a political and strategic spending choice. Immediate national bankruptcy did not compel it.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses G3 affordability, employment effects, Britain's wartime industrial role, and the relative absence of physical devastation.

segments.title: What the treaty stopped each navy building
segments.summary: The cancelled G3s, Tosas, Amagis, Francesco Caracciolos, and Lexingtons reveal that the treaty removed different capabilities from different fleets.
segments.body: For Britain, the G3 battlecruisers matter because a global maritime strategy demanded speed and the ability to threaten trade routes far from home. France had no equally mature modern answer: the Lyon design remained a prewar paper project, while the Normandies had been overtaken by newer foreign work. Japan's Tosa and Amagi projects are treated as more immediately useful losses than a distant next generation. The Francesco Caracciolos might have accelerated the fast-battleship concept because a ship in service would have forced a more urgent response than a paper design. The American loss is framed around the Lexington battlecruisers' long-range cruiser-hunting role, a capability later sought in heavily armed treaty cruisers.

evidence.note: The transcript assesses the British, Japanese, Italian, and American cancelled programmes.

segments.title: Replacement rights and keeping shipyards alive
segments.summary: Treaty replacement clauses shaped fleet tonnage and helped maintain the skilled industrial base needed to build future capital ships.
segments.body: Article 20's retained-ship list gave Britain the right to replace four older 13.5-inch-gun battleships with two new designs, while the United States could finish two Colorados. France and Italy received early-replacement options, while Japan could neither finish its new ships nor obtain comparable replacement rights. Possessing a right to build was not automatically a gain: exercising it meant accepting treaty limits, while waiting could permit more infrastructure preparation or construction after the system weakened. The transcript gives one capital ship every two years as the minimum rhythm for keeping industrial capacity alive at a premium, with Britain and the United States ideally needing two in that period. A pause that looks fiscally economical can impose a larger industrial premium when a navy must restart at speed.

evidence.note: The treaty's replacement arrangements and their industrial implications are compared.

segments.title: Nelson and Rodney as an industrial bridge
segments.summary: The Nelson class illustrates how deliberately paced construction and major refits could preserve British naval-industrial capacity during the treaty gap.
segments.body: Nelson and Rodney matched Nagato's standard displacement while carrying nine 16-inch guns. Ordered and laid down in December 1922, launched in 1925, and commissioned in 1927, their deliberately slow construction spread costs over several years. Industry could not retain armour-making and other specialist capabilities without profitable work, even when the spending did not appear as a steady stream of new battleships. Extensive modernizations of existing ships also sustained yards, facilities, and skills during the long construction gap. Nelson and Rodney therefore served as fleet units and an industrial bridge toward the King George V programme.

evidence.note: The transcript links Nelson and Rodney's construction and later refits to industrial continuity.

segments.title: A faster 15-inch-gun Nelson alternative
segments.summary: A contemporary 15-inch-gun option illustrates the trade between prestige armament and strategic speed in the Nelson design.
segments.body: The video considers replacing the Nelson class's 16-inch battery with 15-inch/50-calibre guns, an option discussed during design. The estimated saving from lighter guns, mountings, and ammunition is roughly 2,200 tons, which could have gone into additional speed. Such a ship might have offered greater strategic mobility, but Britain already retained Hood, Renown, Repulse, and Tiger for fast global work. The final choice can therefore be read as a decision to match other navies' 16-inch status while strengthening the slower battle line.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses the considered 15-inch/50 battery, estimated weight savings, and a possible speed increase.

segments.title: The battle line and fast-raider dilemma
segments.summary: A strong battle line and fast battlecruisers can force an opponent into a damaging choice between concentration and dispersed commerce defence.
segments.body: The video explains why Britain could accept slower Nelson-class ships after retaining Hood, Renown, Repulse, and Tiger for strategic mobility. An enemy that concentrates to face the battle line leaves its trade exposed to fast ships; an enemy that disperses to protect commerce risks defeat in detail. Either response sacrifices something essential, whether commercial protection or fleet survival. The point is a force-structure argument about creating dilemmas instead of matching ship for ship.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Britain’s battle-line and fast-ship strategic combination.

segments.title: Dunkerque and France’s parity problem
segments.summary: The Dunkerque design is read as France’s attempt to reconcile Mediterranean parity with the global demands of empire under treaty limits.
segments.body: France's parity with Italy creates a strategic tension: concentrating in the Mediterranean can weaken imperial coverage, while spreading forces can weaken the balance with Italy. The 26,500-ton Dunkerque concept is presented as an attempt to gain useful numbers and global presence from the available tonnage. Its all-forward arrangement also reflects an effort to obtain an efficient design that French yards could build. The calculation depends on opponents respecting limits, a condition the later Littorios undermined.

evidence.note: The transcript connects Dunkerque, French strategic commitments, and Italian treaty competition.

segments.title: Littorios and Italy’s treaty advantage
segments.summary: The Littorios show how Italy paired a favorable treaty position with a later capital-ship programme that greatly exceeded the stated limits.
segments.body: France's smaller design is contrasted with Littorios approaching 41,000 tons standard displacement and Italy's ability to build four new ships while modernizing old ones. Parity forced a continuing French strategic problem, giving Italy a notable treaty gain even before its later non-compliance. The section also stresses the operational weight of having multiple battleships available together in the Mediterranean. A six-battleship Italian concentration, combined with a comparable German force, could have forced the Royal Navy onto the defensive before British reinforcements entered service.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses Littorio displacement, Italian construction capacity, France–Italy parity, and the reliability of treaty commitments.

segments.title: A twelve-gun Littorio counterfactual
segments.summary: A hypothetical twelve-gun Littorio tests how openly exceeding treaty limits might have changed British gun-calibre choices.
segments.body: The Littorio class is praised as an efficient and sensible Axis capital-ship design, though its nine-gun arrangement looks unfinished after Italy accepted a standard displacement near 41,000 tons. The explicitly hypothetical alternative would fit four triple 15-inch turrets and abandon any pretence of remaining within the treaty. In this counterfactual, a ship launched on that basis in 1937 might have kept the Vickers 14-inch proposal away from Chatfield and the Royal Navy because no equivalent Axis design could plausibly be claimed. The example shows how visible non-compliance and perceived capability can alter another navy's procurement choices.

evidence.note: The transcript labels the twelve-gun Littorio as Dr. Clarke’s hypothetical and connects it to the British 14-inch-gun decision.

segments.title: King George V and British rearmament capacity
segments.summary: The King George V programme is presented as both a cautious treaty-era design choice and proof that British industry could revive large-scale battleship construction.
segments.body: The video links British support for tighter gun limits to a desire for a more peaceful and numerically favorable system. Its illustrative 25,000-ton ceiling would give Britain twenty-one hulls, while Japan would have roughly twelve or thirteen and France and Italy seven each. A shipbuilder from the apprenticeship generation that produced the wartime fleet later described the five King George Vs as warm-ups, a suggestive piece of oral history. Britain ordered all five within a single year before moving toward the Lions and Vanguard. The brief wartime pause in capital-ship and carrier construction shows that stopping a programme can be much easier than restoring its workers, schedules, and momentum. Using the video's post-First World War counting convention, Britain completed eight battleships and the United States ten, while no other treaty power built more than four, exposing the scale gap between their industrial bases.

evidence.note: The transcript covers the smaller-ship numerical case, 14-inch-gun policy, orders for five ships, industrial restart, and postwar construction totals.

segments.title: North Carolinas, Yamatos, and industrial strain
segments.summary: American treaty designs and Japan’s move to Yamato-class battleships show how limits, parity, and industrial capacity shaped very different responses.
segments.body: The North Carolinas are presented as an important bridge to later American battleships, with extensive design work conducted amid the fading treaty system and the gun-calibre debate. Plans could move from 14-inch to 16-inch armament once treaty expectations collapsed, while the completed class established a foundation for later American fast battleships. Japan, by contrast, could not secure parity or orderly replacement rights and then tried to compensate through exceptionally large ships. The Yamato programme shows how a prestige solution can consume industrial capacity needed for other naval tasks. Within technological and economic reason, governments find money for projects they truly prioritize, making Yamato a costly strategic choice rather than a fiscal inevitability.

evidence.note: The transcript compares North Carolina design choices, Japanese parity concerns, Yamato's industrial cost, and government spending priorities.

segments.title: A twelve-gun North Carolina treaty design
segments.summary: An unbuilt 22-knot, twelve-gun North Carolina scheme shows how treaty limits generated ingenious designs that blurred familiar capital-ship categories.
segments.body: Among the many American studies, one Nelson-style layout paired four triple 14-inch turrets with a speed of 22 knots. The design is admired for its engineering economy and potential volume of fire, while its unusual combination earns the description of a battlecarrier by another name. The arrangement was one treaty-constrained study explored before the North Carolina class settled on its completed form. The proposal gives a concrete example of designers trading speed, armament, and layout inside fixed displacement and calibre limits.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the unbuilt 22-knot American design with four triple 14-inch turrets and calls it a battlecarrier by another name.

segments.title: Japan links a 14-inch ceiling to numerical parity
segments.summary: Japan’s conditional offer exposes why gun-calibre limits could not be separated from fleet ratios, geography, and each navy’s strategic burden.
segments.body: During attempts to preserve 14-inch guns as the battleship ceiling, Japan said it would accept the limit only if it received the same number of battleships as Britain and the United States. The other powers would never accept that bargain because Japan's strategic commitments differed from Britain's global obligations and America's two-ocean fleet. Britain also expected American fleet division and congressional underfunding to soften the practical effect of nominal Anglo-American parity. The exchange shows a technical arms-control rule becoming inseparable from force structure, geography, and trust.

evidence.note: The transcript states Japan’s parity condition for accepting a 14-inch ceiling and explains why Britain and the United States would reject it.

segments.title: A Japanese replacement-rights counterfactual
segments.summary: A hypothetical Tosa-and-Amagi replacement programme asks whether controlled construction could have kept Japanese industry active and Japan inside the treaty system.
segments.body: Denying Japan both completion rights and early replacement contributed to industrial discontinuity before the Yamato programme. The proposed alternative would replace older Fusō- and Kongō-family ships with two Tosas and three Amagis while Japan remained inside the treaty framework. This counterfactual was never a Washington Treaty term or a guarantee of peace. The example shows how a limited concession might preserve skills, offer visible status and security, and reduce the incentive to leap from no capital-ship work to building the world's largest battleships.

evidence.note: The transcript proposes a hypothetical replacement of older Japanese ships with two Tosas and three Amagis, then contrasts that path with the Yamato programme.

segments.title: Why treaty controls broke down
segments.summary: The conclusion argues that suppressing both quantitative and qualitative naval competition stored up pressure instead of creating durable security.
segments.body: The treaty system is traced to the trauma of the First World War and an effort to regulate away military competition. Suppressing quantitative and qualitative competition stored up design and construction pressure until the restrictions weakened. Durable limits needed controlled opportunities for states to feel secure and maintain capabilities instead of a complete construction freeze. States did not need to feel strongest, but they did need enough strength to prevent fear and perceived weakness from driving irrational choices. Italy's position is judged comparatively favorable, while American peace aims, British dominance, and Japanese security all failed to produce the outcomes their governments wanted.

evidence.note: The conclusion explains the treaty system's origins, its built-in pressures, and national outcomes.

segments.title: Japanese security fears under the treaty system
segments.summary: Japan's lower ratio and lack of replacement construction are placed within a longer fear of how stronger powers treated weaker states.
segments.body: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance and victory at Tsushima had helped Japan feel secure and recognized as a strong power. The treaty era then allowed the United States to finish Colorados, Britain to build Nelson and Rodney, and France to build Dunkerques while Japan received no comparable capital-ship construction. The argument links the resulting insecurity to Japanese memories of the Spanish-American War and earlier coercion by Western powers, which suggested that strength determined how states could treat one another. The passage does not excuse Japanese violence in China and Korea, but explains how Japanese leaders could interpret imperial aggression as the behavior expected of a strong state.

evidence.note: The transcript links Japan's treaty insecurity to the alliance, Tsushima, Western coercion, the Spanish-American War, and Japanese imperial conduct.

segments.title: Could rolling quotas have saved the treaty system?
segments.summary: The closing thought experiment keeps the historical fleet ratios but permits regular new construction to test whether the treaty might have become more durable.
segments.body: The closing proposal allows Britain and the United States to build five ships in any five-year period, Japan three, and France and Italy two each. This counterfactual was never a provision of the Washington Naval Treaty. It would replace the long building holiday with rolling construction, potentially preserving industrial skills and giving every signatory a visible path to fleet renewal. The video leaves the question open: would controlled construction have made the system more peaceful and more likely to survive, and why?

evidence.note: The transcript gives five-year construction quotas for each treaty ratio and asks whether they would have made the system more peaceful and durable.
